- 只添加经验证真实存在且已发表的引用到 bib + §4

- 分析任务（#16, #17）结果回报给我，我决定如何整合

Synthetic data has become integral to language model training.
Instruction tuning, knowledge distillation, and data augmentation all routinely use model-generated text, and as synthetic corpora are recycled into training pipelines, the process often becomes recursive: each generation of models is fine-tuned on outputs from the previous one.
Recent work demonstrates that such recursive synthetic training triggers \textit{model collapse}, a progressive erosion of distributional tails and downstream capability~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024tails, alemohammad2024mad}.
The problem is especially pressing as web-scraped corpora increasingly contain model-generated content, a trend that introduces implicit recursive loops even without deliberate data reuse.

While model collapse is now well-characterized through theoretical analysis~\citep{dohmatob2024tails} and empirical studies~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024mad}, its effect on the geometric structure of learned representations remains poorly understood.
Characterizing how the embedding space contracts during recursive training could yield computationally cheap collapse indicators from internal model states alone, without text generation or benchmark evaluation.

Current collapse detection depends on downstream metrics such as perplexity and benchmark accuracy, or on analysis of generated text through lexical diversity measures.
Both approaches require either costly inference or external evaluation infrastructure at every generation.
SIGMA~\citep{gu2026sigma} introduced spectral monitoring through embedding covariance analysis and showed that spectral indicators can track collapse, but validated only on OPT-125M over short generation horizons.
Four gaps remain open.
First, no work has systematically characterized spectral dynamics beyond a few generations at 410M+ parameters.
Second, the temporal relationship between spectral indicators and downstream degradation has not been examined.
Third, no study has connected spectral indicators to closed-loop collapse prevention through the lens of early warning signals (EWS)~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Fourth, the relationship between real-data mixing ratios and spectral collapse has not been mapped: it is unknown how much real data suffices to prevent spectral contraction, or whether a sharp phase boundary exists.

We address these gaps by tracking spectral indicators of the embedding matrix across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M-deduped~\citep{biderman2023pythia}, with pilot validation on Pythia-1B-deduped.
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase pattern (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}): spectral decompression (Gen~0--2), where effective rank ($r_{\text{eff}}$) and spectral log-volume (SLV) rise while downstream performance already declines; collapse onset (Gen~2--4), where spectral indicators reverse; and accelerating collapse (Gen~4--10), where contraction accelerates.
Among these indicators, SLV is the most effective for automated monitoring: it requires only a forward pass on held-out data (no text generation), captures distributed volume changes across all spectral directions, and declines monotonically after its peak.
We further design a proportional controller and demonstrate an inherent signal attenuation: moderate real-data mixing prevents the spectral contraction that would trigger the controller, so reactive spectral feedback becomes ineffective precisely when collapse prevention succeeds.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{C1:} The first multi-seed spectral-downstream characterization at 410M+ scale, revealing dynamics invisible in prior short-horizon studies and establishing a reproducible three-phase collapse pattern (decompression, onset, acceleration) across 10 generations (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C2:} SLV as a computationally cheap collapse monitor with monotonic post-peak decline and a HellaSwag-spectral asymmetry: downstream degradation begins during the spectral decompression phase, demonstrating that spectral expansion does not indicate model health (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C3:} Quantitative characterization of signal attenuation under mixing: the spectral controller signal degrades continuously as the real-data fraction approaches $r_{\text{crit}}$ and vanishes entirely above it, a limitation robust to threshold reduction (\S\ref{subsec:controller}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
\end{itemize}
Supporting these findings, we construct a spectral collapse phase diagram across multiple mixing ratios that localizes $r_{\text{crit}}$ empirically, with the bound robust to both the EMA smoothing parameter and random seed (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}, \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}).

3	\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.
4	Scaling laws predict tail erosion as a function of recursive depth~\citep{dohmatob2024tails, dohmatob2024demystified}; the self-consuming loop accelerates collapse even under data accumulation~\citep{alemohammad2024mad}, with as little as 1\% synthetic contamination sufficing~\citep{dohmatob2025strong}, though preserving all prior real data can delay it~\citep{gerstgrasser2024inevitable}.
5	We complement these output/benchmark-based diagnoses by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, requiring no text generation.
6	Unlike neural collapse~\citep{papyan2020prevalence}, which describes last-layer features converging to a simplex ETF in classification, spectral collapse in recursive training reflects progressive embedding volume loss unrelated to class structure.
7	
8	\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
9	Random matrix theory reveals implicit regularization structure in neural network eigenspectra~\citep{martin2021implicit}; effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} quantify representational dimensionality.
10	The spectral decompression phase, in which singular value spread decreases while effective rank increases, resembles the effect of isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual}; recursive fine-tuning may initially reduce the anisotropy documented in standard training~\citep{gao2019representation} before amplifying it during collapse.
11	Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
12	Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
13	Mathematically, our SLV is equivalent to half of SIGMA's $\log\det G$ (both sum log singular values of the embedding matrix), establishing a shared metric foundation.
14	When $n < d$, both metrics face the same rank-deficiency issue; our $\epsilon$-thresholding (\S\ref{subsec:spectral_metrics}) makes the equivalence approximate rather than exact.
15	Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory invisible at SIGMA's 3-generation horizon), and \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}).
16	At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
17	Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.
18	That SIGMA observed analogous spectral shifts on OPT-125M provides preliminary cross-architecture evidence for the generality of spectral collapse dynamics.
19	
20	\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
21	Early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originate in ecology, where rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}, with detection methods ranging from statistical tests~\citep{dakos2012methods} to deep learning~\citep{bury2021deeplearning}.
22	A central tension is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}.
23	Rate-induced critical transitions~\citep{siteur2016ecosystems} further demonstrate that interventions can themselves alter system dynamics.
24	We encounter a parallel tension: real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}), unlike ecological stabilization which preserves signal direction; our contribution is quantifying how rapidly this signal degrades across mixing ratios.
25	\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.
26	
27	\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
28	Data composition significantly affects LM quality~\citep{longpre2024pretrainer, muennighoff2023scaling}, and several methods optimize domain mixtures through proxy models or predictive formulas~\citep{xie2023doremi, ye2025mixinglaws, chen2025aioli}.
29	These approaches evaluate mixing through loss or benchmarks.
30	Our work reveals a complementary dimension: real-vs-synthetic mixing reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}) that loss-based metrics do not capture, and our controller targets recursive spectral collapse rather than general domain balance.

1	\subsection{Spectral Metrics}
2	\label{subsec:spectral_metrics}
3	
4	Given a language model at generation $t$, we extract last-layer embeddings for $n{=}1{,}000$ held-out samples to form $\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$.
5	Let $\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_{\min(n,d)}$ denote the singular values of $\mathbf{E}$.
6	We track three complementary spectral indicators:
7	
8	\paragraph{Spectral Log-Volume (SLV).}
9	$\text{SLV} = \sum_{i:\,\sigma_i > \epsilon} \log \sigma_i$, where $\epsilon = 10^{-10}$ excludes numerically zero components.
10	When $n < d$ (as in our setting with $n{=}1{,}000$, $d{=}1{,}024$), $\mathbf{E}$ has at most $n$ non-zero singular values; SLV thus measures the log-volume of the occupied subspace rather than the full $d$-dimensional space.
11	Because it sums over all non-negligible singular values, SLV is sensitive to contraction along any spectral direction, not only the dominant ones.
12	
13	\paragraph{Effective Rank.}
14	$r_{\text{eff}} = \exp(H(\mathbf{p}))$, where $p_i = \sigma_i / \sum_j \sigma_j$ and $H$ is the Shannon entropy, measuring how many dimensions carry substantial variance (uniform $\to d$, concentrated $\to 1$).
15	
16	\paragraph{Leading Singular Value.}
17	$\sigma_1$ tracks the dominant spectral direction; rising $\sigma_1$ under falling $r_{\text{eff}}$ signals representational collapse into a low-dimensional subspace.
18	
19	\subsection{Adaptive Mixing Controller}
20	\label{subsec:controller}
21	
22	We propose a closed-loop controller that adjusts the real-data mixing ratio $r_t$ at each generation based on the rate of spectral change.
23	The update rule is:
24	\begin{equation}
25	\label{eq:controller}
26	r_{t+1} = \operatorname{clip}\!\bigl(\tfrac{B_{\text{rem}}}{T - t} + k \cdot \max(0,\,\Delta_t - \tau),\; r_{\min},\, r_{\max}\bigr)
27	\end{equation}
28	where $B_{\text{rem}}$ is the remaining real-data budget (fraction of total budget not yet consumed), $T$ is the total number of generations, $\tau{=}0.002$ is a sensitivity threshold, and $k{=}10$ is the controller gain.
29	The signal $\Delta_t$ is the baseline-normalized SLV drop: $\Delta_t = (\widetilde{S}_{t-1} - \widetilde{S}_t) / |\widetilde{S}_0|$, where $\widetilde{S}_t$ is the exponential moving average (EMA)-smoothed SLV ($\alpha{=}0.5$) and $\widetilde{S}_0$ is initialized from the pretrained model (Gen~0, SLV${=}2366.68$).
30	The signed form ensures that spectral decompression ($\Delta_t < 0$) does not trigger the controller; only contraction activates the $\max(0, \cdot)$ gate in Eq.~\ref{eq:controller}.
31	The output is clipped to $[r_{\min}, r_{\max}] = [0.20, 0.80]$ and subject to $\sum_t r_t \leq B_{\text{total}}$.
32	The lower bound ensures a minimum synthetic fraction; $r_{\max}$ defines the controller's operational range.
33	
34	The first term distributes the remaining budget uniformly across future generations; the model degrades gracefully even without spectral signal.
35	The second term injects additional real data when SLV contraction exceeds the threshold $\tau$, proportional to the severity of the spectral drop.
36	This design requires no lookahead and operates with a single hyperparameter choice ($k$) beyond the budget constraint.
37	
38	\paragraph{Controller Silence Condition.}
39	Define $r_{\text{crit}}$ as the minimum constant mixing ratio such that the EMA-smoothed SLV is non-decreasing from the second generation onward: $\widetilde{S}_t \geq \widetilde{S}_{t-1}$ for all $t \in \{2, \ldots, T\}$ (excluding the initial fine-tuning transient at $t{=}1$). For conditions with multiple seeds, the condition is evaluated on the cross-seed mean trajectory.
40	When a constant ratio $r \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ is applied, $\Delta_t \leq 0 < \tau$ for all $t \geq 2$ and any $\tau > 0$, so the controller boost is identically zero.
41	This $\tau$-independence means the signal attenuation cannot be resolved by lowering the sensitivity threshold; the same argument extends to cumulative variants.
42	Our experiments (\S\ref{subsec:phase1}) empirically bound $0.25 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.3$ over Gen~2--10 for Pythia-410M on OpenWebText.
43	
44	\paragraph{Second-Order Extension.}
45	\label{subsec:second_order}
46	A natural extension monitors the rate of change of the controller signal itself:
47	\begin{equation}
48	\label{eq:second_order}
49	\Delta^2_t = \widetilde{\Delta}_{t-1} - \widetilde{\Delta}_t
50	\end{equation}
51	where $\widetilde{\Delta}_t$ is the EMA-smoothed first-order signal ($\alpha_2{=}0.3$).
52	A sustained negative $\Delta^2_t$ indicates decelerating SLV growth, a potential precursor to stagnation even when SLV is still rising.
53	We evaluate this indicator in \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}.
54	
55	\subsection{Collapse Phase Diagram}
56	\label{subsec:phase_diagram}
57	
58	We define the \emph{collapse phase diagram} as the mapping from constant mixing ratio $r$ to the SLV trajectory over $T$ generations.
59	For each $r$, we classify the outcome: \emph{collapse} if SLV declines monotonically after the decompression phase (Gen~2 onward), \emph{stable} if SLV is non-decreasing, and \emph{transitional} if SLV shows non-monotonic behavior after Gen~2 (both increases and decreases within the observation window).

Spectral contraction accelerates: the mean per-generation $r_{\text{eff}}$ decline in Phase~III is $1.78 \pm 0.22$\%/gen (mean $\pm$ s.d.\ across three seeds).
By Gen~10, $r_{\text{eff}}$ falls to 438.1 ($-$11.7\% from peak), SLV drops to 2181.4 ($-$7.8\% from baseline), perplexity reaches 71.0 ($+$643\%), and $\sigma_1$ reverses its earlier decline, reaching 874.6 at Gen~10, a sign of renewed spectral concentration (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}).

\paragraph{Cross-Scale Pilot.}
Repeating the protocol on Pythia-1B (Gen~0--3) confirms the same decompression-onset structure ($r_{\text{eff}}$ peak at Gen~2, SLV peak one generation earlier). SLV's low cost and monotonic post-peak decline make it well-suited as an automated collapse monitor.
In our setup, SLV computation (1{,}000-sample forward pass plus SVD of the $n {\times} d$ embedding matrix) takes ${<}\,1$~second on a single GPU, whereas HellaSwag 0-shot evaluation requires ${\sim}70$~minutes end-to-end under identical hardware.

\subsection{Adaptive Mixing Comparison}
\label{subsec:phase1}

Under pure synthetic training (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}), SLV peaks at Gen~2 (2468) and declines monotonically; with 50\% mixing, SLV rises to 2573 at Gen~10 (105 points above the pure-collapse peak), with only a negligible Gen~1 dip ($\Delta_1 \approx 0.0003$, well below $\tau$).

The adaptive controller ($k{=}10$) remains silent through all ten generations: $\max \Delta_t = 0.0003$ at Gen~1, well below $\tau{=}0.002$, and $\Delta_t \leq 0$ for all $t \geq 2$.
Since the controller monitors the \emph{rate} of spectral change, even moderate mixing that does not prevent downstream degradation (PPL $+$45\% at $r{=}0.2$) suffices to suppress the signal.
Pure collapse produces SLV decline from Gen~3 while $r{=}0.5$ yields sustained growth, bounding $0.2 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.5$ (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}).

Despite sustained spectral expansion, downstream metrics degrade steadily: perplexity increases 59\% ($9.55 \to 15.20$) and distinct-4 falls 87\% ($.74 \to .095$) over ten generations, the lowest D-4 of any condition, below even pure collapse ($r{=}0$: 0.324).
This reinforces the asymmetry from \S\ref{subsec:phase0}: spectral health under mixed training does not guarantee model health, and signal attenuation renders per-generation reactive controllers ineffective precisely when collapse prevention succeeds.
The relationship between $r_{\text{crit}}$ and signal suppression is inherent to any rate-based indicator; our empirical contribution is demonstrating that this creates a continuous, quantifiable degradation of monitoring capability across the sub-critical regime, a phenomenon not previously quantified.
This raises the question: is signal attenuation specific to SLV, or does it affect all candidate EWS indicators?

\subsection{Alternative EWS Comparison}
\label{subsec:alt_ews}

We compare SLV against six alternative collapse indicators from three signal sources: embedding geometry (RankMe, isotropy), attention weights (stable rank, spectral norm), and output distributions (token entropy, perplexity growth rate).

Table~\ref{tab:ews_comparison} summarizes the comparison under pure-synthetic training ($r{=}0$).
Two indicators share SLV's decompression-then-collapse trajectory: RankMe~\citep{rankme2023}, the exponential of the normalized singular-value entropy, peaks at Gen~2 and declines monotonically thereafter, though with 2.5$\times$ lower signal-to-noise ratio (4.7\% relative change vs.\ 11.8\% for SLV).
Weight-level and output-level indicators (stable rank, spectral norm, token entropy) change monotonically from Gen~0 with no decompression phase; they cannot distinguish collapse onset from the initial fine-tuning transient.
Isotropy is the least reliable indicator: random sampling without a fixed seed introduces approximately 5\% variance, and it exhibits six monotonicity violations across ten generations, with direction reversals at Gen~4+ that produce a misleading recovery signal.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcrrc@{}}
\toprule
Indicator & Source & Peak & Mono? & Rel $\Delta$ & Rev.? \\
\midrule
SLV         & emb-SVD   & Gen 2 & \checkmark & 11.8\% & \checkmark \\
RankMe      & emb-SVD   & Gen 2 & \checkmark &  4.7\% & \checkmark \\
Token ent.  & logit     & ---   & \checkmark &  9.6\% & \checkmark \\
Stable rank & attn wt.  & ---   & \checkmark & 14.0\% & \checkmark \\
Spec.\ norm & attn wt.  & ---   & \checkmark &  8.0\% & \checkmark \\
Isotropy    & emb       & ---   & $\times$\,(6) & 75\%   & \checkmark \\
PPL growth  & ppl       & ---   & $\sim$\,(1) &  ---   & \checkmark \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Alternative early warning indicators under pure-synthetic training ($r{=}0$, Pythia-410M, 10 gen). \textbf{Peak}: generation at which the indicator reverses (--- = monotonic from Gen~0). \textbf{Mono?}: post-peak monotonicity (\checkmark\ = yes; number = violations). \textbf{Rel $\Delta$}: $|v_{10} - v_0|/|v_0|$, magnitude of total relative change Gen~0--10. \textbf{Rev.?}: direction reversal under $r{=}0.5$ mixing (\checkmark\ = reversed).}
\label{tab:ews_comparison}
\end{table}

The final column of Table~\ref{tab:ews_comparison} reveals that all seven indicators reverse direction under 50\% real-data mixing.
This universality confirms that signal attenuation (\S\ref{subsec:controller}) is not specific to SLV: any per-generation reactive controller based on these indicators will fall silent when mixing exceeds $r_{\text{crit}}$.
Among embedding-level metrics, SLV offers the highest signal-to-noise ratio (2.5$\times$ that of RankMe) and, together with RankMe, is the only indicator that exhibits a decompression baseline to distinguish collapse onset from training transients.
SLV is the only indicator that combines decompression-phase sensitivity, post-peak monotonicity, and sub-second computation cost; it shares a metric foundation with SIGMA's $\log\det G$ ($= 2 \times \text{SLV}$; \S\ref{sec:related}).

\subsection{Collapse Phase Diagram}
\label{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}

We now map SLV trajectories across mixing ratios to construct the collapse phase diagram defined in \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}.
Figure~\ref{fig:phase_diagram} plots SLV across 10 recursive generations for five mixing ratios; three qualitatively distinct trajectory types emerge:

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/phase_diagram.pdf}
\caption{SLV trajectories across mixing ratios (Pythia-410M; $r{=}0$ and $r{=}0.25$: 3-seed mean; $r{=}0.3$: 3-seed mean; $r{=}0.2$ and $r{=}0.5$: single seed). Type~I ($r{=}0$): decompression then monotonic collapse. Type~II ($r{=}0.2$, $r{=}0.25$): transient dip followed by recovery. Type~III ($r{=}0.3$, $r{=}0.5$): monotonic expansion from Gen~2 onward. The shaded band marks the critical threshold $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$. The dashed horizontal line indicates the Gen~0 baseline.}
\label{fig:phase_diagram}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Type~I: Pure Collapse ($r{=}0$).}
SLV exhibits large decompression ($+$97 points at Gen~1, peaking at Gen~2) followed by accelerating contraction (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).

\paragraph{Type~II: Near-critical Mixing ($r{=}0.2$).}
Twenty percent real data suppresses the SLV decompression phase: SLV rises only 0.78 points from Gen~0 to Gen~1 (vs.\ $+$98 under $r{=}0$), dips at Gen~2 ($2367.5 \to 2358.3$, $-9.2$).
Recovery begins at Gen~3, with per-generation gains accelerating from $+4.2$ to $+30.9$ (Gen~6) before moderating, reaching 2479.7 at Gen~10 ($+4.8\%$ above baseline).
Because $\widetilde{S}_2 = 2362.7 < \widetilde{S}_1 = 2367.1$ (EMA-smoothed SLV; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), the non-decreasing condition is violated and $r{=}0.2$ formally lies below $r_{\text{crit}}$.
The trajectory is consistent with the transitional regime (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}): initial contraction followed by sustained recovery over the full 10-generation horizon.
The smoothed signal never exceeds the controller threshold ($\max \Delta_t = 0.0019$ at Gen~2, below $\tau = 0.002$), so as little as 20\% real data silences the controller entirely.
The effective rank still rises at Gen~2 ($476.7 \to 481.6$) while the EMA-smoothed SLV registers a net decline ($\widetilde{S}_2 < \widetilde{S}_1$), evidence that smoothed SLV detects spectral contraction earlier at this mixing ratio.

At $r{=}0.25$, the full 10-generation trajectory follows the same Type~II pattern: SLV dips from Gen~0 to Gen~1 ($2366.7 \to 2362.1$, $-4.6$; seed~42, representative trajectory), reaches a minimum at Gen~2 ($2363.1$), then rises monotonically through Gen~10 (three-seed mean $2488.1$, $+5.1\%$ above baseline).
The EMA-smoothed sequence confirms the sub-critical classification: $\widetilde{S}_1 = 2364.4$, $\widetilde{S}_2 = 2363.8$, satisfying $\widetilde{S}_2 < \widetilde{S}_1$ and violating the non-decreasing condition.
Controller silence is more pronounced than at $r{=}0.2$: $\max \Delta_t = 0.00028 < \tau = 0.002$, a $6.7\times$ weaker signal than the $r{=}0.2$ maximum ($0.0019$), consistent with further signal attenuation as the real-data fraction increases.
The amplitude of the EMA violation at $r{=}0.25$ varies substantially across seeds ($\widetilde{S}_2 - \widetilde{S}_1 = -0.6$, $-1.7$, $-0.9$), consistent with the elevated fluctuations expected near a phase boundary, while trajectories at $r{=}0$ and $r \geq 0.3$ show low cross-seed variance ($< 0.5\%$).

\paragraph{Type~III: Super-critical Mixing ($r \geq 0.3$).}
SLV rises monotonically from Gen~2 onward, reaching 2573 at Gen~10 ($+$8.7\% above baseline), consistent with $r{=}0.5 \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
Per-generation gains remain positive through all post-transient generations ($\Delta_t \in [+11, +35]$ for $t \geq 2$; mean $+23.0$), sustaining expansion with no reversal toward the contraction trajectory of Type~I within the observed horizon.

These three types partition the mixing-ratio axis into sub-critical ($r < r_{\text{crit}}$), transitional, and stable ($r \geq r_{\text{crit}}$) zones.
Type classification is based solely on spectral trajectory shape; downstream metrics such as D-4 may diverge, as demonstrated by the non-monotonic D-4 pattern across mixing ratios (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}).
At $r{=}0.3$, SLV expands monotonically from Gen~2 to 2508.2 at Gen~10 ($+$6.0\% above baseline), with sustained positive growth across all eight post-transient generations.
This confirms $r{=}0.3 \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ over the full 10-generation horizon, tightening the bound to $0.25 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.3$.
Across three seeds, one individual EMA-smoothed trajectory shows a transient violation of 0.83~points at Gen~2; the remaining two satisfy non-decreasing from $t \geq 2$. The cross-seed mean trajectory is non-decreasing at all post-transient generations (Gen~10 SLV CV $= 0.12\%$), confirming the Type~III classification.
The critical threshold is robust to the smoothing parameter: recomputing the EMA-smoothed SLV for $\alpha \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.7\}$ yields $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$ in all cases, with the non-decreasing condition violated at Gen~2 for $r \leq 0.25$ and satisfied on the cross-seed mean for $r \geq 0.3$ regardless of $\alpha$.

The largest single-generation SLV drop in the first two generations shrinks with $r$: $-9.2$ at $r{=}0.2$ (Gen~1$\to$2), $-4.6$ at $r{=}0.25$ (Gen~0$\to$1; seed~42), and $-0.6$ at $r{=}0.3$ (Gen~0$\to$1), consistent with a continuous crossover rather than a sharp boundary.
The Type~II trajectory clarifies what $r_{\text{crit}}$ marks in practice: not a boundary between collapse and stability in final outcome, but a transition in trajectory shape.
Below $r_{\text{crit}}$, real-data mixing fails to suppress the initial SLV contraction transient but sustains spectral expansion through Gen~10 once the transient passes.

\paragraph{Output Diversity Divergence.}
At $r{=}0.2$, D-4 exhibits a V-shaped recovery (0.438 at Gen~5 $\to$ 0.520 at Gen~10), but this pattern does not generalize: at $r{=}0.25$, D-4 declines monotonically to 0.342 despite comparable SLV recovery, indicating that spectral expansion does not guarantee diversity restoration.
More broadly, D-4 exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with $r$: it peaks at $r{=}0.2$ (.520), exceeds the pure-collapse baseline (.324) at $r \leq 0.25$ but drops below it at $r \geq 0.3$, reaching .095 at $r{=}0.5$, the lowest across all conditions (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}).
This pattern is consistent with increasing real-data anchoring: at high $r$, the model converges toward the fixed real-data distribution, producing coherent but stylistically homogeneous text.
This divergence between spectral health (monotonically improving with $r$) and n-gram diversity underscores that SLV and D-4 capture orthogonal aspects of model behavior.
D-4 exhibits substantially higher cross-seed variance than spectral metrics: at $r{=}0$ (s.d.\ $= 0.15$ vs.\ SLV s.d.\ $= 28$, a ${>}30\times$ lower coefficient of variation for SLV) and $r{=}0.3$ (s.d.\ $= 0.155$ vs.\ SLV s.d.\ $= 2.9$; Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}), suggesting that n-gram diversity reflects stochastic generation choices rather than the deterministic geometric structure captured by SLV.
This pattern generalizes across mixing ratios: at $r{=}0.25$, SLV cross-seed CV is 0.12\% versus 3.9\% for D-4, confirming that spectral geometry captures a deterministic structural property largely independent of stochastic training noise.

Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary} consolidates the final-generation metrics across all five mixing ratios.

\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}clrrrrrc@{}}
\toprule
$r$ & Type & SLV & $r_{\text{eff}}$ & PPL & D-4 & $\max\Delta_t$ & Gen. \\
\midrule
0    & I   & 2181.4 & 438.1 & 71.0\phantom{0} & .324 & ---   & 10 \\
0.20 & II  & 2479.7 & 511.3 & 13.83 & .520 & .0019 & 10 \\
0.25 & II  & 2488.1 & 513.8 & 13.41 & .342 & .0003 & 10 \\
0.30 & III & 2508.2 & 521.1 & 13.35 & .295 & 0     & 10 \\
0.50 & III & 2573.2 & 554.5 & 15.20 & .095 & 0     & 10 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Final-generation spectral and downstream metrics across mixing ratios (all runs to Gen~10). $\max\Delta_t$ computed for $t \geq 2$, excluding the initial fine-tuning transient. Type classification follows \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}. $r{=}0$ reports the mean of three seeds (42, 43, 44); $r{=}0.3$ the mean of three seeds (42, 43, 44); $r{=}0.2$ and $r{=}0.5$ report a single seed; $r{=}0.25$ the mean of three seeds (42, 43, 44). D-4 exhibits high cross-seed variance at $r{=}0$ (s.d.\ $= 0.15$) and $r{=}0.3$ (s.d.\ $= 0.155$).}
\label{tab:phase_summary}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Second-order and alternative triggers.}
A second-order acceleration indicator $\Delta^2_t$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:second_order}) does not discriminate between sub- and super-critical regimes: all trajectories exhibit negative $\Delta^2_t$ in late generations regardless of mixing ratio.
A level-based trigger keyed to baseline SLV could detect the transient dip in Type~II trajectories, but would not activate under Type~III where SLV exceeds baseline at all generations.
Finer resolution between 0.25 and 0.3 would narrow the $r_{\text{crit}}$ bound but would not change the practical recommendation to set $r$ above 0.3.
For practitioners, the phase diagram provides a direct prescription: in our setting, setting $r > 0.3$ prevents spectral collapse without per-generation monitoring.

Tracking embedding spectral properties across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M reveals that model collapse follows a structured three-phase geometric trajectory, with the decompression-to-onset structure confirmed at 1B; full 10-generation validation at this scale remains future work.
Of the indicators we examined, SLV offers the most effective monitoring signal: sub-second computation via a single forward pass, monotonic post-peak decline, and sensitivity to distributed spectral contraction before it manifests as reduced effective rank.
Crucially, downstream degradation begins during the decompression phase, demonstrating that spectral expansion does not indicate model health.
A collapse phase diagram across five mixing ratios localizes $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$: above this threshold SLV expands monotonically (Type~III), while just below it a transitional regime (Type~II) exhibits an initial contraction transient followed by recovery.

A proportional controller exposes inherent signal attenuation: the controller signal vanishes at $r \geq 0.3$, and because all seven EWS indicators reverse under sufficient mixing (\S\ref{subsec:alt_ews}), any reactive controller faces this prevention--detectability tradeoff~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Nevertheless, spectral indicators reveal whether the current ratio lies in the transitional or stable zone without waiting for downstream degradation.

Although reactive controllers fail under signal attenuation, calibrating $r_{\text{crit}}$ once and setting $r > r_{\text{crit}}$ as a static mixing floor reduces collapse prevention to a one-time offline calibration via forward-pass spectral checks.
However, spectral stability does not guarantee downstream quality: even at $r = 0.5$, perplexity increases 59\% and D-4 drops 87\% (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}); quality degradation at fixed $r$ is nonetheless gradual and predictable, unlike the accelerating degradation under spectral collapse.

Signal attenuation instantiates the classical EWS intervention--loss tradeoff~\citep{scheffer2009ews} via a distinct mechanism---trajectory inversion rather than declining signal-to-noise ratio---and may extend to implicit-loop settings where web corpora contain model-generated content; validating this generalization is future work.

# Response Letter — Round 2 Revision

---

## Summary of Changes

We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. In this revision, we have:

1. **Expanded seed coverage** from 1–2 seeds to 3 seeds for all critical mixing ratios (r=0, 0.25, 0.3), demonstrating cross-seed reproducibility with spectral metric CV < 1.3%.
2. **Added per-generation variance analysis** (Appendix Table 4) showing seed-level variation across all 11 generations.
3. **Clarified the SLV definition** and its relationship to SIGMA (§2.1, §4).
4. **Refined the signal attenuation framing** from "limitation" to "structural characterization" (§4.3).
5. **Added missing baselines and literature** (Dohmatob et al. 2024, Gerstgrasser et al. 2024).
6. **Corrected the SLV mathematical definition** to a pseudo-log-determinant with ε-threshold, resolving the n < d rank-deficiency issue (§2.1).
7. **Qualified the 1B pilot claim scope** (§4.1).
8. **Added n-sensitivity analysis** to Limitations.
9. **Downgraded C4** from core contribution to supporting text.
10. **Fixed conclusion overclaim** ("sidestepping entirely" → qualified language with downstream quality caveat).

---

## Response to Reviewer 1

### R1-W1: Critical mixing ratio granularity

> "The critical mixing ratio is localized only to (0.25, 0.3], which is a coarse bound."

We agree that finer resolution (e.g., r = 0.27, 0.28, 0.29) would narrow the bound, and we note this as natural future work. However, the current resolution is sufficient for three reasons:

1. **Practical insensitivity**: Practitioners need a safe threshold, not a precise critical point. Setting r > 0.3 prevents spectral collapse regardless of whether r_crit is 0.26 or 0.29.

2. **Robustness across seeds and smoothing**: The qualitative boundary is consistent across 3 seeds at r=0, 0.25, and 0.3, and across 3 EMA smoothing parameters (α ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}): r=0.25 consistently shows Type II trajectories (transitional), while r=0.3 consistently shows Type III (stable).

3. **Typology over precision**: The phase diagram's contribution is the trajectory typology itself — distinguishing collapse, transitional, and stable regimes — rather than a precise critical constant.

4. **Continuous crossover evidence**: The largest single-generation SLV dip shrinks monotonically with r (−9.2 at r=0.2, −4.6 at r=0.25, −0.6 at r=0.3), indicating a continuous crossover rather than a sharp phase transition. This makes the precise r_crit value less practically significant than the trajectory type classification.

Our 0.05 mixing-ratio resolution is comparable to typical domain-mixing studies (e.g., DoReMi, Aioli use 0.05–0.1 increments); finer resolution is natural future work but does not change the practical recommendation.

### R1-W2: Variance across random seeds

> "Most experiments use a single seed."

We have expanded seed coverage significantly in this revision:

| Mixing ratio | Seeds | Status | SLV CV (Gen 10) |
|-------------|-------|--------|-----------------|
| r = 0 | 42, 43, 44 | ✅ Complete | 1.3% |
| r = 0.25 | 42, 43, 44 | ✅ Complete | 0.12% |
| r = 0.3 | 42, 43, 44 | ✅ Complete | 0.12% |
| r = 0.2 | 42, 43 | ✅ Complete (Type II confirmed both seeds) | SLV CV 1.0%; D-4 high inter-seed variance (.520 vs .245) consistent with §3.5 |
| r = 0.5 | 42 | ✅ Complete; seed 43 pending | — (single seed; 2-seed pending) |

The critical boundary conditions (r=0.25 and r=0.3) now have full 3-seed coverage. Per-generation variance is reported in Appendix Table 4. Spectral metrics show low cross-seed variance (CV < 1.3%), confirming that spectral collapse is a deterministic structural phenomenon rather than a seed-dependent artifact.

### R1-N2: Seed replication (novelty concern)

Addressed jointly with R1-W2 above. The expanded 3-seed coverage at the phase boundary (r=0.25, r=0.3) confirms:
- Type II classification at r=0.25 is seed-independent (all 3 seeds show dip-then-recovery with EMA violation at Gen 1–2)
- Type III classification at r=0.3 is seed-independent (all 3 seeds show monotonic SLV expansion)
- The r_crit ∈ (0.25, 0.3] bound holds across all seeds

### C1 Strengthening via Multi-Seed Replication

Our 3-seed results strengthen C1 from a preliminary observation to a well-replicated empirical finding: the spectral peak at Gen 2 is identical across all 3 seeds, SLV CV is < 1.3% at every generation (11 checkpoints × 3 seeds), and Phase III decline rate is 1.78 ± 0.22%/gen (relative s.d. = 12%). In contrast, D-4 CV reaches 46% at Gen 10 (36× higher), confirming that spectral geometry captures deterministic structure while text-level metrics reflect stochastic generation choices.

---

## Response to Reviewer 2

### R2-N2: SIGMA equivalence

> "SLV appears equivalent to existing SIGMA metric."

We now honestly disclose this relationship in §2.1 and §4 (Related Work): SLV = ½ × SIGMA's log det(G). Our contributions are independent of metric novelty:
- The three-phase trajectory typology
- The phase diagram with critical threshold characterization
- The signal attenuation phenomenon under mixing

### R2-W2: Missing literature

Added Dohmatob et al. (2024) and Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) to Related Work with explicit positioning.

---

## Anticipated Concern: C3 Novelty (Signal Attenuation)

> Potential attack: "Signal attenuation is trivially expected — preventing collapse removes the signal."

The observation that intervention suppresses warning signals is anticipated by the EWS literature (Scheffer 2009, Siteur 2016). Our contribution is not the qualitative observation but three quantitative findings:

1. **Continuous degradation**: Signal attenuation is not binary. The controller signal degrades *continuously* as r → r_crit — from strong decline under pure collapse (r=0) through attenuated (r=0.2, Δ_max=0.002) to silence (r≥0.3, Δ_max<0.0003). This continuous relationship across 5 ratios (with 3 seeds at the boundary conditions r=0, 0.25, and 0.3) has not been quantified before.

2. **τ-independence**: The signal vanishes above r_crit for *any* positive threshold τ, not just our chosen τ=0.002. This is structural, not a sensitivity issue.

3. **Cross-indicator generality**: All 7 EWS indicators exhibit the same attenuation. The phenomenon is not metric-specific but geometric.

We acknowledge that controller silence above r_crit follows from the controller's design (the non-decreasing condition is the contrapositive of the trigger condition). Our empirical contributions are orthogonal to this definitional relationship: (a) the *continuous degradation* of signal strength below r_crit (Δ_max shrinks from scenarios where SLV declines sharply (r=0, no mixing) through attenuated signal (r=0.2, Δ_max=0.002) to near-silence (r=0.25, Δ_max=0.0003) and complete silence (r≥0.3)), which is not deducible from the binary silence condition; (b) *τ-independence* — the signal vanishes for any positive threshold, a structural property not obvious from the design; and (c) *cross-indicator universality* — all 7 EWS indicators exhibit the same attenuation, extending the phenomenon beyond the SLV-based controller to any rate-based spectral monitor.

---

## Answers to Reviewer Questions

**Q1 (SLV implementation)**: SLV is computed as Σ log σ_i for σ_i > ε (ε=10⁻¹⁰) on the SVD of the embedding matrix E ∈ ℝⁿˣᵈ, not the Gram matrix. This is now clarified in §2.1.

**Q2 (Per-seed values)**: Per-generation per-seed values are now reported in Appendix Table 4 (11 generations × 6 metrics × 3 seeds = 198 data points).

**Q3 (r=0.3 seed 43 EMA values)**: S̃₁ = 2365.29, S̃₂ = 2364.46, yielding S̃₂ − S̃₁ = −0.83 (a transient violation in this individual seed). However, the cross-seed mean trajectory satisfies the non-decreasing condition at all generations, consistent with Type III classification.

**Q4 (exp_013/014 results)**: Complete. Table 1 now reports 3-seed means for r=0 (seeds 42, 43, 44). r=0.25 also has full 3-seed coverage. The r_crit conclusion is unchanged.

**Q5 (D-4 at r=0.5)**: D-4 drops to 0.095 at r=0.5 due to real-data anchoring: at high r, the model converges toward the fixed real-data distribution, producing coherent but stylistically homogeneous text. This asymmetry between spectral health and output diversity is discussed in §3.5 "Output Diversity Divergence."

---

## Additional Revisions (not prompted by reviewers)

- Fixed D-4 baseline comparison logic (§4.1, L163)
- Corrected CV multiplier notation (L166)
- Added "cross-seed robust" characterization in §4.1
- Compressed Δ²_t discussion per page limit

---

Tracking embedding spectral properties across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M reveals that model collapse follows a structured three-phase geometric trajectory, with the decompression-to-onset structure confirmed at 1B; full 10-generation validation at this scale remains future work.
Of the indicators we examined, SLV offers the most effective monitoring signal: sub-second computation via a single forward pass, monotonic post-peak decline, and sensitivity to distributed spectral contraction before it manifests as reduced effective rank.
Crucially, downstream degradation begins during the decompression phase, demonstrating that spectral expansion does not indicate model health.
A collapse phase diagram across five mixing ratios localizes $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$: above this threshold SLV expands monotonically (Type~III), while just below it a transitional regime (Type~II) exhibits an initial contraction transient followed by recovery.

A proportional controller exposes inherent signal attenuation: the controller signal vanishes at $r \geq 0.3$, and because all seven EWS indicators reverse under sufficient mixing (\S\ref{subsec:alt_ews}), any reactive controller faces this prevention--detectability tradeoff~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Nevertheless, spectral indicators reveal whether the current ratio lies in the transitional or stable zone without waiting for downstream degradation.

Although reactive controllers fail under signal attenuation, calibrating $r_{\text{crit}}$ once and setting $r > r_{\text{crit}}$ as a static mixing floor reduces collapse prevention to a one-time offline calibration via forward-pass spectral checks.
However, spectral stability does not guarantee downstream quality: even at $r = 0.5$, perplexity increases 59\% and D-4 drops 87\% (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}); quality degradation at fixed $r$ is nonetheless gradual and predictable, unlike the accelerating degradation under spectral collapse.

Signal attenuation instantiates the classical EWS intervention--loss tradeoff~\citep{scheffer2009ews} via a distinct mechanism---trajectory inversion rather than declining signal-to-noise ratio---and may extend to implicit-loop settings where web corpora contain model-generated content; validating this generalization is future work.

Synthetic data has become integral to language model training.
Instruction tuning, knowledge distillation, and data augmentation all routinely use model-generated text, and as synthetic corpora are recycled into training pipelines, the process often becomes recursive: each generation of models is fine-tuned on outputs from the previous one.
Recent work demonstrates that such recursive synthetic training triggers \textit{model collapse}, a progressive erosion of distributional tails and downstream capability~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024tails, alemohammad2024mad}.
The problem is especially pressing as web-scraped corpora increasingly contain model-generated content, a trend that introduces implicit recursive loops even without deliberate data reuse.

While model collapse is now well-characterized through theoretical analysis~\citep{dohmatob2024tails} and empirical studies~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024mad}, its effect on the geometric structure of learned representations remains poorly understood.
Characterizing how the embedding space contracts during recursive training could yield computationally cheap collapse indicators from internal model states alone, without text generation or benchmark evaluation.

Current collapse detection depends on downstream metrics such as perplexity and benchmark accuracy, or on analysis of generated text through lexical diversity measures.
Both approaches require either costly inference or external evaluation infrastructure at every generation.
SIGMA~\citep{gu2026sigma} introduced spectral monitoring through embedding covariance analysis and showed that spectral indicators can track collapse, but validated only on OPT-125M over short generation horizons.
Four gaps remain open.
First, no work has systematically characterized spectral dynamics beyond a few generations at 410M+ parameters.
Second, the temporal relationship between spectral indicators and downstream degradation has not been examined.
Third, no study has connected spectral indicators to closed-loop collapse prevention through the lens of early warning signals (EWS)~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Fourth, the relationship between real-data mixing ratios and spectral collapse has not been mapped: it is unknown how much real data suffices to prevent spectral contraction, or whether a sharp phase boundary exists.

We address these gaps by tracking spectral indicators of the embedding matrix across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M-deduped~\citep{biderman2023pythia}, with pilot validation on Pythia-1B-deduped.
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase pattern (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}): spectral decompression (Gen~0--2), where effective rank ($r_{\text{eff}}$) and spectral log-volume (SLV) rise while downstream performance already declines; collapse onset (Gen~2--4), where spectral indicators reverse; and accelerating collapse (Gen~4--10), where contraction accelerates.
Among these indicators, SLV is the most effective for automated monitoring: it requires only a forward pass on held-out data (no text generation), captures distributed volume changes across all spectral directions, and declines monotonically after its peak.
We further design a proportional controller and demonstrate an inherent signal attenuation: moderate real-data mixing prevents the spectral contraction that would trigger the controller, so reactive spectral feedback becomes ineffective precisely when collapse prevention succeeds.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{C1:} The first multi-seed spectral-downstream characterization at 410M+ scale, revealing dynamics invisible in prior short-horizon studies and establishing a reproducible three-phase collapse pattern (decompression, onset, acceleration) across 10 generations (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C2:} SLV as a computationally cheap collapse monitor with monotonic post-peak decline and a HellaSwag-spectral asymmetry: downstream degradation begins during the spectral decompression phase, demonstrating that spectral expansion does not indicate model health (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C3:} Quantitative characterization of signal attenuation under mixing: the spectral controller signal degrades continuously as the real-data fraction approaches $r_{\text{crit}}$ and vanishes entirely above it, a limitation robust to threshold reduction (\S\ref{subsec:controller}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
\end{itemize}
Supporting these findings, we construct a spectral collapse phase diagram across multiple mixing ratios that localizes $r_{\text{crit}}$ empirically, with the bound robust to both the EMA smoothing parameter and random seed (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}, \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}).

10	When $n < d$ (as in our setting with $n{=}1{,}000$, $d{=}1{,}024$), $\mathbf{E}$ has at most $n$ non-zero singular values; SLV thus measures the log-volume of the occupied subspace rather than the full $d$-dimensional space.
11	Because it sums over all non-negligible singular values, SLV is sensitive to contraction along any spectral direction, not only the dominant ones.
12	
13	\paragraph{Effective Rank.}
14	$r_{\text{eff}} = \exp(H(\mathbf{p}))$, where $p_i = \sigma_i / \sum_j \sigma_j$ and $H$ is the Shannon entropy, measuring how many dimensions carry substantial variance (uniform $\to d$, concentrated $\to 1$).
15	
16	\paragraph{Leading Singular Value.}

19	\subsection{Adaptive Mixing Controller}
20	\label{subsec:controller}
21	
22	We propose a closed-loop controller that adjusts the real-data mixing ratio $r_t$ at each generation based on the rate of spectral change.
23	The update rule is:
24	\begin{equation}
25	\label{eq:controller}
26	r_{t+1} = \operatorname{clip}\!\bigl(\tfrac{B_{\text{rem}}}{T - t} + k \cdot \max(0,\,\Delta_t - \tau),\; r_{\min},\, r_{\max}\bigr)
27	\end{equation}
28	where $B_{\text{rem}}$ is the remaining real-data budget (fraction of total budget not yet consumed), $T$ is the total number of generations, $\tau{=}0.002$ is a sensitivity threshold, and $k{=}10$ is the controller gain.
29	The signal $\Delta_t$ is the baseline-normalized SLV drop: $\Delta_t = (\widetilde{S}_{t-1} - \widetilde{S}_t) / |\widetilde{S}_0|$, where $\widetilde{S}_t$ is the exponential moving average (EMA)-smoothed SLV ($\alpha{=}0.5$) and $\widetilde{S}_0$ is initialized from the pretrained model (Gen~0, SLV${=}2366.68$).
30	The signed form ensures that spectral decompression ($\Delta_t < 0$) does not trigger the controller; only contraction activates the $\max(0, \cdot)$ gate in Eq.~\ref{eq:controller}.
31	The output is clipped to $[r_{\min}, r_{\max}] = [0.20, 0.80]$ and subject to $\sum_t r_t \leq B_{\text{total}}$.
32	The lower bound ensures a minimum synthetic fraction; $r_{\max}$ defines the controller's operational range.
33	
34	The first term distributes the remaining budget uniformly across future generations; the model degrades gracefully even without spectral signal.
35	The second term injects additional real data when SLV contraction exceeds the threshold $\tau$, proportional to the severity of the spectral drop.
36	This design requires no lookahead and operates with a single hyperparameter choice ($k$) beyond the budget constraint.
37	
38	\paragraph{Controller Silence Condition.}
39	Define $r_{\text{crit}}$ as the minimum constant mixing ratio such that the EMA-smoothed SLV is non-decreasing from the second generation onward: $\widetilde{S}_t \geq \widetilde{S}_{t-1}$ for all $t \in \{2, \ldots, T\}$ (excluding the initial fine-tuning transient at $t{=}1$). For conditions with multiple seeds, the condition is evaluated on the cross-seed mean trajectory.
40	When a constant ratio $r \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ is applied, $\Delta_t \leq 0 < \tau$ for all $t \geq 2$ and any $\tau > 0$, so the controller boost is identically zero.
41	This $\tau$-independence means the signal attenuation cannot be resolved by lowering the sensitivity threshold; the same argument extends to cumulative variants.
42	Our experiments (\S\ref{subsec:phase1}) empirically bound $0.25 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.3$ over Gen~2--10 for Pythia-410M on OpenWebText.
43	
44	\paragraph{Second-Order Extension.}
45	\label{subsec:second_order}
46	A natural extension monitors the rate of change of the controller signal itself:
47	\begin{equation}
48	\label{eq:second_order}
49	\Delta^2_t = \widetilde{\Delta}_{t-1} - \widetilde{\Delta}_t
50	\end{equation}
51	where $\widetilde{\Delta}_t$ is the EMA-smoothed first-order signal ($\alpha_2{=}0.3$).
52	A sustained negative $\Delta^2_t$ indicates decelerating SLV growth, a potential precursor to stagnation even when SLV is still rising.
53	We evaluate this indicator in \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}.

55	\subsection{Collapse Phase Diagram}
56	\label{subsec:phase_diagram}
57	
58	We define the \emph{collapse phase diagram} as the mapping from constant mixing ratio $r$ to the SLV trajectory over $T$ generations.
59	For each $r$, we classify the outcome: \emph{collapse} if SLV declines monotonically after the decompression phase (Gen~2 onward), \emph{stable} if SLV is non-decreasing, and \emph{transitional} if SLV shows non-monotonic behavior after Gen~2 (both increases and decreases within the observation window).
60	The critical mixing ratio $r_{\text{crit}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:controller}) is the boundary between collapse and stability in this diagram.
61	We estimate $r_{\text{crit}}$ by evaluating multiple constant ratios and identifying the lowest $r$ for which $\widetilde{S}_t \geq \widetilde{S}_{t-1}$ holds for all $t \in \{2, \ldots, T\}$.

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{subsec:setup}

We use the publicly released final Pythia-410M-deduped checkpoint \citep{biderman2023pythia} as our base model and fine-tune on a 50K-subset of OpenWebText.
Starting from the pretrained checkpoint (generation~0), each subsequent generation fine-tunes on synthetic text produced by the previous generation, for a total of 10 recursive generations.
At each generation we compute the spectral indicators from \S\ref{subsec:spectral_metrics} on 1K held-out last-layer embeddings, paired with three downstream metrics: perplexity, HellaSwag accuracy (0-shot), and distinct-4.
These three metrics (language modeling capability, natural language understanding, and generation diversity) cover the primary evaluation dimensions accessible to a 410M-parameter model.

For the mixing comparison (\S\ref{subsec:phase1}), we evaluate three strategies sharing the same total real-data budget:
(1)~\textbf{pure collapse} ($r_t{=}0$),
(2)~\textbf{fixed mix} ($r_t{=}0.50$), and
(3)~\textbf{adaptive} ($k{=}10$, Eq.~\ref{eq:controller}).
To construct the collapse phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}), we additionally evaluate fixed mixing at $r \in \{0.2, 0.25, 0.3\}$.

\subsection{Spectral Collapse Characterization}
\label{subsec:phase0}

Table~\ref{tab:phase0} reports spectral and downstream metrics across 10 recursive generations, which reveal a three-phase structure.

\begin{figure}[t]

\caption{SLV across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M (solid: $r{=}0$, 3-seed mean; dashed: $r{=}0.5$, single seed) under pure-synthetic training and 50\% real-data mixing. Three phases are visible in the pure-synthetic trajectory: decompression (Gen~0--2, SLV peaks at 2468), onset (Gen~2--4), and acceleration (Gen~4--10, SLV falls 11\% from peak to 2181). Under 50\% mixing, SLV rises monotonically (except a negligible Gen~1 dip) to 2573 at Gen~10, 8.7\% above baseline and 105 points above the pure-collapse peak.}
\label{fig:spectral_trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Phase I: Spectral Decompression (Gen~0--2).}
In the first two generations, $r_{\text{eff}}$ rises from 417.6 to 496.2 (+18.8\%) and SLV increases from 2366.7 to 2468.0 (+4.3\%), while $\sigma_1$ drops sharply from 1942.8 to 718.7 as spectral mass redistributes from the dominant direction to smaller components.
The consistency of the peak position (Gen~2 across all three seeds) and its coincidence with the qualitative reversal of $\sigma_1$ dynamics (from declining to rising) suggest that the phase boundary reflects a structural transition rather than a statistical artifact.
Crucially, this decompression does not indicate improved model quality: HellaSwag drops from 0.413 to 0.380 ($-$8.0\%) and distinct-4 falls from 0.738 to 0.505 ($-$31.6\%) during the same interval.
HellaSwag already declines 5.4\% from Gen~0 to Gen~1, precisely when spectral indicators are still rising; this asymmetry suggests that decompression captures distributional broadening rather than preservation of task-supporting representations.
A monitoring system relying solely on spectral metrics during Phase~I would incorrectly conclude the model remains healthy; joint spectral-downstream tracking~\citep{gu2026sigma} is advisable.
SLV's value lies not in temporal precedence but in computational efficiency ($<$1\,s vs.\ ${\sim}$70\,min for benchmarks) and cross-seed robustness (CV $< 1.3\%$).

\paragraph{Phase II: Collapse Onset (Gen~2--4).}
Both $r_{\text{eff}}$ and SLV reverse after Gen~2 ($r_{\text{eff}}$: 496.2$\to$493.6, SLV: 2468$\to$2440), and this reversal marks the transition from decompression to collapse while perplexity continues its monotonic rise.

\paragraph{Phase III: Accelerating Collapse (Gen~4--10).}
Spectral contraction accelerates: the mean per-generation $r_{\text{eff}}$ decline in Phase~III is $1.78 \pm 0.22$\%/gen (mean $\pm$ s.d.\ across three seeds).
By Gen~10, $r_{\text{eff}}$ falls to 438.1 ($-$11.7\% from peak), SLV drops to 2181.4 ($-$7.8\% from baseline), perplexity reaches 71.0 ($+$643\%), and $\sigma_1$ reverses its earlier decline, reaching 874.6 at Gen~10, a sign of renewed spectral concentration (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}).

\paragraph{Cross-Scale Pilot.}
Repeating the protocol on Pythia-1B (Gen~0--3) confirms the same decompression-onset structure ($r_{\text{eff}}$ peak at Gen~2, SLV peak one generation earlier). SLV's low cost and monotonic post-peak decline make it well-suited as an automated collapse monitor.
In our setup, SLV computation (1{,}000-sample forward pass plus SVD of the $n {\times} d$ embedding matrix) takes ${<}\,1$~second on a single GPU, whereas HellaSwag 0-shot evaluation requires ${\sim}70$~minutes end-to-end under identical hardware.

\subsection{Adaptive Mixing Comparison}
\label{subsec:phase1}

Under pure synthetic training (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}), SLV peaks at Gen~2 (2468) and declines monotonically; with 50\% mixing, SLV rises to 2573 at Gen~10 (105 points above the pure-collapse peak), with only a negligible Gen~1 dip ($\Delta_1 \approx 0.0003$, well below $\tau$).

The adaptive controller ($k{=}10$) remains silent through all ten generations: $\max \Delta_t = 0.0003$ at Gen~1, well below $\tau{=}0.002$, and $\Delta_t \leq 0$ for all $t \geq 2$.
Since the controller monitors the \emph{rate} of spectral change, even moderate mixing that does not prevent downstream degradation (PPL $+$45\% at $r{=}0.2$) suffices to suppress the signal.
Pure collapse produces SLV decline from Gen~3 while $r{=}0.5$ yields sustained growth, bounding $0.2 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.5$ (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}).

Despite sustained spectral expansion, downstream metrics degrade steadily: perplexity increases 59\% ($9.55 \to 15.20$) and distinct-4 falls 87\% ($.74 \to .095$) over ten generations, the lowest D-4 of any condition, below even pure collapse ($r{=}0$: 0.324).
This reinforces the asymmetry from \S\ref{subsec:phase0}: spectral health under mixed training does not guarantee model health, and signal attenuation renders per-generation reactive controllers ineffective precisely when collapse prevention succeeds.
The relationship between $r_{\text{crit}}$ and signal suppression is inherent to any rate-based indicator; our empirical contribution is demonstrating that this creates a continuous, quantifiable degradation of monitoring capability across the sub-critical regime, a phenomenon not previously quantified.
This raises the question: is signal attenuation specific to SLV, or does it affect all candidate EWS indicators?

\subsection{Alternative EWS Comparison}
\label{subsec:alt_ews}

We compare SLV against six alternative collapse indicators from three signal sources: embedding geometry (RankMe, isotropy), attention weights (stable rank, spectral norm), and output distributions (token entropy, perplexity growth rate).

Table~\ref{tab:ews_comparison} summarizes the comparison under pure-synthetic training ($r{=}0$).
Two indicators share SLV's decompression-then-collapse trajectory: RankMe~\citep{rankme2023}, the exponential of the normalized singular-value entropy, peaks at Gen~2 and declines monotonically thereafter, though with 2.5$\times$ lower signal-to-noise ratio (4.7\% relative change vs.\ 11.8\% for SLV).
Weight-level and output-level indicators (stable rank, spectral norm, token entropy) change monotonically from Gen~0 with no decompression phase; they cannot distinguish collapse onset from the initial fine-tuning transient.
Isotropy is the least reliable indicator: random sampling without a fixed seed introduces approximately 5\% variance, and it exhibits six monotonicity violations across ten generations, with direction reversals at Gen~4+ that produce a misleading recovery signal.

The final column of Table~\ref{tab:ews_comparison} reveals that all seven indicators reverse direction under 50\% real-data mixing.
This universality confirms that signal attenuation (\S\ref{subsec:controller}) is not specific to SLV: any per-generation reactive controller based on these indicators will fall silent when mixing exceeds $r_{\text{crit}}$.
Among embedding-level metrics, SLV offers the highest signal-to-noise ratio (2.5$\times$ that of RankMe) and, together with RankMe, is the only indicator that exhibits a decompression baseline to distinguish collapse onset from training transients.
SLV is the only indicator that combines decompression-phase sensitivity, post-peak monotonicity, and sub-second computation cost; it shares a metric foundation with SIGMA's $\log\det G$ ($= 2 \times \text{SLV}$; \S\ref{sec:related}).

\subsection{Collapse Phase Diagram}
\label{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}

We now map SLV trajectories across mixing ratios to construct the collapse phase diagram defined in \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}.
Figure~\ref{fig:phase_diagram} plots SLV across 10 recursive generations for five mixing ratios; three qualitatively distinct trajectory types emerge:

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/phase_diagram.pdf}
\caption{SLV trajectories across mixing ratios (Pythia-410M; $r{=}0$ and $r{=}0.25$: 3-seed mean; $r{=}0.3$: 3-seed mean; $r{=}0.2$ and $r{=}0.5$: single seed). Type~I ($r{=}0$): decompression then monotonic collapse. Type~II ($r{=}0.2$, $r{=}0.25$): transient dip followed by recovery. Type~III ($r{=}0.3$, $r{=}0.5$): monotonic expansion from Gen~2 onward. The shaded band marks the critical threshold $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$. The dashed horizontal line indicates the Gen~0 baseline.}
\label{fig:phase_diagram}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Type~I: Pure Collapse ($r{=}0$).}
SLV exhibits large decompression ($+$97 points at Gen~1, peaking at Gen~2) followed by accelerating contraction (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).

\paragraph{Type~II: Near-critical Mixing ($r{=}0.2$).}
Twenty percent real data suppresses the SLV decompression phase: SLV rises only 0.78 points from Gen~0 to Gen~1 (vs.\ $+$98 under $r{=}0$), dips at Gen~2 ($2367.5 \to 2358.3$, $-9.2$).
Recovery begins at Gen~3, with per-generation gains accelerating from $+4.2$ to $+30.9$ (Gen~6) before moderating, reaching 2479.7 at Gen~10 ($+4.8\%$ above baseline).
Because $\widetilde{S}_2 = 2362.7 < \widetilde{S}_1 = 2367.1$ (EMA-smoothed SLV; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), the non-decreasing condition is violated and $r{=}0.2$ formally lies below $r_{\text{crit}}$.
The trajectory is consistent with the transitional regime (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}): initial contraction followed by sustained recovery over the full 10-generation horizon.
The smoothed signal never exceeds the controller threshold ($\max \Delta_t = 0.0019$ at Gen~2, below $\tau = 0.002$), so as little as 20\% real data silences the controller entirely.
The effective rank still rises at Gen~2 ($476.7 \to 481.6$) while the EMA-smoothed SLV registers a net decline ($\widetilde{S}_2 < \widetilde{S}_1$), evidence that smoothed SLV detects spectral contraction earlier at this mixing ratio.

At $r{=}0.25$, the full 10-generation trajectory follows the same Type~II pattern: SLV dips from Gen~0 to Gen~1 ($2366.7 \to 2362.1$, $-4.6$; seed~42, representative trajectory), reaches a minimum at Gen~2 ($2363.1$), then rises monotonically through Gen~10 (three-seed mean $2488.1$, $+5.1\%$ above baseline).
The EMA-smoothed sequence confirms the sub-critical classification: $\widetilde{S}_1 = 2364.4$, $\widetilde{S}_2 = 2363.8$, satisfying $\widetilde{S}_2 < \widetilde{S}_1$ and violating the non-decreasing condition.
Controller silence is more pronounced than at $r{=}0.2$: $\max \Delta_t = 0.00028 < \tau = 0.002$, a $6.7\times$ weaker signal than the $r{=}0.2$ maximum ($0.0019$), consistent with further signal attenuation as the real-data fraction increases.
The amplitude of the EMA violation at $r{=}0.25$ varies substantially across seeds ($\widetilde{S}_2 - \widetilde{S}_1 = -0.6$, $-1.7$, $-0.9$), consistent with the elevated fluctuations expected near a phase boundary, while trajectories at $r{=}0$ and $r \geq 0.3$ show low cross-seed variance ($< 0.5\%$).

\paragraph{Type~III: Super-critical Mixing ($r \geq 0.3$).}
SLV rises monotonically from Gen~2 onward, reaching 2573 at Gen~10 ($+$8.7\% above baseline), consistent with $r{=}0.5 \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
Per-generation gains remain positive through all post-transient generations ($\Delta_t \in [+11, +35]$ for $t \geq 2$; mean $+23.0$), sustaining expansion with no reversal toward the contraction trajectory of Type~I within the observed horizon.

These three types partition the mixing-ratio axis into sub-critical ($r < r_{\text{crit}}$), transitional, and stable ($r \geq r_{\text{crit}}$) zones.
Type classification is based solely on spectral trajectory shape; downstream metrics such as D-4 may diverge, as demonstrated by the non-monotonic D-4 pattern across mixing ratios (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}).
At $r{=}0.3$, SLV expands monotonically from Gen~2 to 2508.2 at Gen~10 ($+$6.0\% above baseline), with sustained positive growth across all eight post-transient generations.
This confirms $r{=}0.3 \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ over the full 10-generation horizon, tightening the bound to $0.25 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.3$.
Across three seeds, one individual EMA-smoothed trajectory shows a transient violation of 0.83~points at Gen~2; the remaining two satisfy non-decreasing from $t \geq 2$. The cross-seed mean trajectory is non-decreasing at all post-transient generations (Gen~10 SLV CV $= 0.12\%$), confirming the Type~III classification.
The critical threshold is robust to the smoothing parameter: recomputing the EMA-smoothed SLV for $\alpha \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.7\}$ yields $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$ in all cases, with the non-decreasing condition violated at Gen~2 for $r \leq 0.25$ and satisfied on the cross-seed mean for $r \geq 0.3$ regardless of $\alpha$.

The largest single-generation SLV drop in the first two generations shrinks with $r$: $-9.2$ at $r{=}0.2$ (Gen~1$\to$2), $-4.6$ at $r{=}0.25$ (Gen~0$\to$1; seed~42), and $-0.6$ at $r{=}0.3$ (Gen~0$\to$1), consistent with a continuous crossover rather than a sharp boundary.
The Type~II trajectory clarifies what $r_{\text{crit}}$ marks in practice: not a boundary between collapse and stability in final outcome, but a transition in trajectory shape.
Below $r_{\text{crit}}$, real-data mixing fails to suppress the initial SLV contraction transient but sustains spectral expansion through Gen~10 once the transient passes.

\paragraph{Output Diversity Divergence.}
At $r{=}0.2$, D-4 exhibits a V-shaped recovery (0.438 at Gen~5 $\to$ 0.520 at Gen~10), but this pattern does not generalize: at $r{=}0.25$, D-4 declines monotonically to 0.342 despite comparable SLV recovery, indicating that spectral expansion does not guarantee diversity restoration.
More broadly, D-4 exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with $r$: it peaks at $r{=}0.2$ (.520), exceeds the pure-collapse baseline (.324) at $r \leq 0.25$ but drops below it at $r \geq 0.3$, reaching .095 at $r{=}0.5$, the lowest across all conditions (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}).
This pattern is consistent with increasing real-data anchoring: at high $r$, the model converges toward the fixed real-data distribution, producing coherent but stylistically homogeneous text.
This divergence between spectral health (monotonically improving with $r$) and n-gram diversity underscores that SLV and D-4 capture orthogonal aspects of model behavior.
D-4 exhibits substantially higher cross-seed variance than spectral metrics: at $r{=}0$ (s.d.\ $= 0.15$ vs.\ SLV s.d.\ $= 28$, a ${>}30\times$ lower coefficient of variation for SLV) and $r{=}0.3$ (s.d.\ $= 0.155$ vs.\ SLV s.d.\ $= 2.9$; Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}), suggesting that n-gram diversity reflects stochastic generation choices rather than the deterministic geometric structure captured by SLV.
This pattern generalizes across mixing ratios: at $r{=}0.25$, SLV cross-seed CV is 0.12\% versus 3.9\% for D-4, confirming that spectral geometry captures a deterministic structural property largely independent of stochastic training noise.

3	\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.

5	We complement these output/benchmark-based diagnoses by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, requiring no text generation.
6	Unlike neural collapse~\citep{papyan2020prevalence}, which describes last-layer features converging to a simplex ETF in classification, spectral collapse in recursive training reflects progressive embedding volume loss unrelated to class structure.

8	\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
9	Random matrix theory reveals implicit regularization structure in neural network eigenspectra~\citep{martin2021implicit}; effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} quantify representational dimensionality.
10	The spectral decompression phase, in which singular value spread decreases while effective rank increases, resembles the effect of isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual}; recursive fine-tuning may initially reduce the anisotropy documented in standard training~\citep{gao2019representation} before amplifying it during collapse.
11	Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
12	Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
13	Mathematically, our SLV is equivalent to half of SIGMA's $\log\det G$ (both sum log singular values of the embedding matrix), establishing a shared metric foundation.
14	When $n < d$, both metrics face the same rank-deficiency issue; our $\epsilon$-thresholding (\S\ref{subsec:spectral_metrics}) makes the equivalence approximate rather than exact.
15	Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory invisible at SIGMA's 3-generation horizon), and \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}).
16	At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
17	Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.
18	That SIGMA observed analogous spectral shifts on OPT-125M provides preliminary cross-architecture evidence for the generality of spectral collapse dynamics.

20	\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
21	Early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originate in ecology, where rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}, with detection methods ranging from statistical tests~\citep{dakos2012methods} to deep learning~\citep{bury2021deeplearning}.
22	A central tension is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}.
23	Rate-induced critical transitions~\citep{siteur2016ecosystems} further demonstrate that interventions can themselves alter system dynamics.
24	We encounter a parallel tension: real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}), unlike ecological stabilization which preserves signal direction; our contribution is quantifying how rapidly this signal degrades across mixing ratios.
25	\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.
26	
27	\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
28	Data composition significantly affects LM quality~\citep{longpre2024pretrainer, muennighoff2023scaling}, and several methods optimize domain mixtures through proxy models or predictive formulas~\citep{xie2023doremi, ye2025mixinglaws, chen2025aioli}.
29	These approaches evaluate mixing through loss or benchmarks.
30	Our work reveals a complementary dimension: real-vs-synthetic mixing reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}) that loss-based metrics do not capture, and our controller targets recursive spectral collapse rather than general domain balance.

The spectral decompression phase, in which singular value spread decreases while effective rank increases, resembles the effect of isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual}; recursive fine-tuning may initially reduce the anisotropy documented in standard training~\citep{gao2019representation} before amplifying it during collapse.
Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
Mathematically, our SLV is equivalent to half of SIGMA's $\log\det G$ (both sum log singular values of the embedding matrix), establishing a shared metric foundation.
When $n < d$, both metrics face the same rank-deficiency issue; our $\epsilon$-thresholding (\S\ref{subsec:spectral_metrics}) makes the equivalence approximate rather than exact.
Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory invisible at SIGMA's 3-generation horizon), and \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}).
At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.
That SIGMA observed analogous spectral shifts on OPT-125M provides preliminary cross-architecture evidence for the generality of spectral collapse dynamics.

\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
Early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originate in ecology, where rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}, with detection methods ranging from statistical tests~\citep{dakos2012methods} to deep learning~\citep{bury2021deeplearning}.
A central tension is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}.
Rate-induced critical transitions~\citep{siteur2016ecosystems} further demonstrate that interventions can themselves alter system dynamics.
We encounter a parallel tension: real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}), unlike ecological stabilization which preserves signal direction; our contribution is quantifying how rapidly this signal degrades across mixing ratios.
\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.

\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
Data composition significantly affects LM quality~\citep{longpre2024pretrainer, muennighoff2023scaling}, and several methods optimize domain mixtures through proxy models or predictive formulas~\citep{xie2023doremi, ye2025mixinglaws, chen2025aioli}.
These approaches evaluate mixing through loss or benchmarks.
Our work reveals a complementary dimension: real-vs-synthetic mixing reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}) that loss-based metrics do not capture, and our controller targets recursive spectral collapse rather than general domain balance.

2	\label{sec:limitations}
